spans.text: There is a moment near the beginning of this novel when a rich young man sits down to a friendly game of cards and, over the course of a single evening, loses his fortune, his will, and command of his own voice. He cannot say afterward what happened to him. He knows only that a calm elderly stranger with large grey eyes sat across the table, and that somewhere between the deal and the turn of a card his mind was no longer his own. That scene is the whole book in miniature. Dr. Mabuse, der Spieler is a novel about a man who plays other people the way a cardsharp plays a deck, and about a society so shaken that it could imagine itself being played.

Mabuse is one of the great villains of the twentieth century, and like most great villains he outgrew the book that made him. He is a physician, a hypnotist, a master of disguise, a forger, a speculator, and a murderer, and he is none of these things for their own sake. What he wants is dominion: the private, absolute rule of one will over everything around it. He counterfeits money and counterfeits himself with equal ease, appearing as an old gentleman, a drunk, a Dutch professor, a Bavarian laborer, dissolving one identity and assuming the next. Ranged against him is State Prosecutor Wenk, who hunts him through gambling dens and séance parlors and out onto the water in a chase that turns the placid landscape of southern Germany into a nightmare. The pursuit is real and gripping. But the novel's deeper subject is the thing Mabuse embodies, and to understand that, it helps to know when and where he was born.
Norbert Jacques

Norbert Jacques was born on 6 June 1880 in Luxembourg-Eich, a district of Luxembourg City, and he wrote not in French or Luxembourgish but in German. He studied briefly and restlessly, abandoned the law, and made his way as a journalist and travel writer before settling in Berlin around 1910. He was a prolific, worldly, second-tier man of letters, the author of adventure novels and travel books, when in the early 1920s he invented the character who would eclipse everything else he ever wrote. Dr. Mabuse, der Spieler was a sensation. It reportedly sold well over half a million copies in Germany, an almost unheard-of figure for its day, and it made Mabuse a household name while the ink was barely dry. Jacques received German citizenship in 1922, at the height of the book's success.

His later life darkened the picture. From 1940 onward, in occupied Luxembourg, Jacques is reported to have lent his pen to German cultural propaganda, and after the war he was accused of collaboration, held in custody, and, reportedly, expelled from his homeland in 1946. He died in Koblenz in 1954, largely forgotten, unable to find a publisher for the criminal genius who had once made him famous. It is one of the ironies of literary history that the creator of a figure of total, amoral will should have ended his own life on the wrong side of that theme. The novel stands apart from its author's biography, but a modern reader deserves to have the whole of it.
A picture of the time

The book appeared at the turn of 1921 to 1922, serialized first in the Berliner Illustrirte Zeitung and then published in book form, in an expanded version, by the great house of Ullstein. It arrived at a raw and dangerous moment. Germany had lost the war three years earlier; the young Weimar Republic was besieged from left and right, shaken by coup attempts and political assassinations, and its currency was beginning the slide that would end, in 1923, in the most famous hyperinflation in history. That catastrophe still lay a little in the future when Jacques was writing, but the fear of it, the sense of a world in which money and meaning were coming loose from their moorings, was already in the air. Mabuse is a creature of exactly that anxiety. He rigs the stock exchange, floods the country with forged notes, and treats the economy as one more table to be worked. When Fritz Lang filmed the novel, he subtitled the first part Ein Bild der Zeit,
"A Picture of the Time,"

and the phrase is precise. Readers recognized in Mabuse not a fantasy but a diagnosis: the unseen manipulator behind the visible chaos, the man who profits from a society that no longer trusts its own ground.
The title itself carries the theme. Der Spieler means
"the gambler,"

but the German word opens outward: a Spieler is also a player in the sense of one who plays a part, an actor, and one who plays others, a manipulator pulling strings. Mabuse is all three at once, and the novel never lets the senses separate. Gambling, performance, and domination are one activity for him, and the reader is meant to feel the vertigo of a man for whom the whole world is a game with no rules but his own advantage.
The Mabuse afterlife

Mabuse escaped the page almost immediately. Fritz Lang's monumental two-part silent film, Dr. Mabuse, der Spieler, premiered in Berlin in the spring of 1922, its first part opening on 27 April, only months after the novel's own publication. Adapted by Thea von Harbou, who married Lang that same year, the film runs to nearly four and a half hours and stands today as a landmark of Weimar cinema. It is a free adaptation rather than a faithful one: von Harbou and Lang cut the interior monologues that suit prose and not silent film, dropped Mabuse's South American ambitions, and added the elaborate counterfeiting intrigue for which the film is now remembered. What they kept was the essential menace, the sense of a single malign intelligence orchestrating a whole society from the shadows.

Lang was not finished with him. In 1933 he made Das Testament des Dr. Mabuse, in which he put Nazi-flavored rhetoric into the mouth of a criminal madman; the film was banned by Goebbels's ministry before it could open in Germany and premiered instead in Budapest. Nearly three decades later, in 1960, Lang returned one last time for Die 1000 Augen des Dr. Mabuse,
"The Thousand Eyes of Dr. Mabuse,"

his final film as a director, which relocated the master manipulator to the surveillance-haunted world of postwar Germany and launched a whole series of 1960s sequels. Mabuse has proven to be exactly the kind of figure his creator imagined: one who never quite dies, only changes his face and reappears in the anxieties of a new age.
Why a new translation
English readers have had only one way into this novel, and it has not served them well. In 1923 George Allen & Unwin published Dr. Mabuse, Master of Mystery,
authorized translation by Lilian A. Clare.

It was the first English version and, for a century, the only one, and it begins its distortions with the title: der Spieler, the Gambler, the word that holds the book's whole meaning, is simply gone, replaced by a bland
"Master of Mystery."

The losses go far deeper than the cover. Clare was working for an Edwardian readership and translated accordingly, softening, tidying, and censoring as she went. Where Jacques writes that a prostitute has been murdered, Clare gives us a
"woman of the streets."
Where a prisoner's lips are broken open against the iron bars of a cell, she invents a
"crowbar."
An entire sexual assault at the climax of one chapter is quietly dropped and rewritten so that the man
"could not do it,"

reversing the meaning outright. This is not an isolated prudishness but a habit: Jacques's violence and sexuality are repeatedly muffled, and his fever cooled into something more genteel than he ever intended.

Just as damaging is what Clare does to the novel's mind. Count Told collects Expressionist art, and Expressionism is one of the book's keywords, a shorthand for the hysterical, money-drunk modern culture Jacques is anatomizing; Clare systematically replaces it with
"Futurist,"
blurring the very diagnosis the novel is making. Elsewhere she softens a psychiatrist into a man
"interested in hypnotism,"
collapses Jacques's paired coinage
"politics of the mind, politics of the soul"
into a single phrase, and mishears names throughout, so that the Countess Dusy becomes
"Lucy"
and Mabuse's imagined South American kingdom of Eitopomar becomes
"Citopomar."
In several passages she does not merely soften the German but inverts it, so that characters end up meaning the opposite of what they say.

This edition goes back to the original German text and translates it fresh, from first page to last, restoring what a century of readers has been missing: the plainness of the violence, the heat of the prose, the exactness of the ideas. Every chapter was rendered from the German and then checked, meaning by meaning, against the historical record of the earlier version, keeping whatever the original supports.
A note on the text

One small scholarly repair should be mentioned. The original Ullstein printing contains a printer's error in its chapter numbering: the numerals V and XVI were skipped, leaving nineteen numbered chapters where the author plainly wrote twenty-one, with the missing breaks surviving only as unmarked gaps in the text. This edition restores the full twenty-one-chapter structure, dividing the two oversized chapters at exactly the points the narrative and the early records confirm. A few of the author's own inconsistencies have been quietly regularized, and his fierce, headlong style has been kept intact rather than smoothed into modern thriller prose. What follows is Norbert Jacques's Dr. Mabuse, the Gambler, in English, whole, for the first time.

The distinguished old gentleman introduced himself. As usual, nobody caught the name. But he was elegant, dressed in discreet cloth of the finest quality. For a tiepin he wore a single white pearl, a little baroque, but of the whiteness of a blonde woman's back, as Karstens put it, and he laid something like twenty thousand marks on the gaming table in front of him straightaway.
Young Hull, scion of an industrial fortune running to millions, in which his father let him share generously, had brought him along.
Play began at once. With a silent bow the guest accepted the game that was proposed: twenty-one. The stakes were unlimited. Ritter held the bank first.
At first the play showed nothing unusual at all. Loss and gain went around the table.

But soon it began: Hull was losing. It began almost at the very moment the turn to hold the bank came to the old gentleman. Hull lost hundred-mark notes at first. He played calmly, resigned to his bad luck. In front of the old gentleman, smaller notes began to mingle with the pile of thousands he had laid out before him.

Only outwardly did Hull play calmly. Inside he was in a hot agitation. Veils drifted back and forth before his brain. His notes chasséed across to the guest without his really noticing. His senses were as if coated with a fine, invisible spiderweb that hemmed him in more and more.

He drank a few cognacs and then had a bottle of champagne brought. But it helped nothing further than this: he changed compartments in his wallet and reached for the thousands. He had fetched them from the bank that afternoon.

His bad luck at play grew improbable. When he had good cards, it seemed to him that out of some corner of his inner self shrouded in darkness a warning hand laid itself on his mouth. He came down from the height of his stakes and named a trifling sum.
The old gentleman was now due to pass the bank on. But he offered, for Hull's sake, to keep it a while yet. He said:

If the gentlemen agree, I shall keep the bank a few rounds more. You see how the money piles up in front of me. I am the guest of your gracious club. Make allowance for my painful feelings toward Herr Hull, and grant me what I ask of you.
But though it was said in a modest form of speech, it sounded imperious, pushing aside any refusal.
The club servant eyed the guest with suspicion. But the man was playing with cards the club itself supplied, freshly broken from their wrappers every time.

The game threw fire into the circle. There was heavy drinking, too. A light intoxication spun itself around the table. The guest did not exclude himself from the drinking. He behaved in no way conspicuously. He had a calm gaze that lingered long in every eye that looked at him, large gray eyes with something masterful about them, eyes that scarcely seemed to follow the game. His hands were large, massive, and calm, as if they were made of wood. The others, much younger men, their fingers already trembled with the reflection of an inner excitement.
Hull played on, though he could feel his wallet growing thinner and thinner.

What is the matter? he kept asking himself. He wanted to stand up and let a hand pass by, to take some air at a window and look out for once into the stillness of the night, from which he hoped to breathe in a stream of calm for himself. But he sat as if fettered to the leather, pressed his elbows into the red felt, and all his thoughts fell out of him, uncontrolled, into a void, as into the dimensionless space of sleep.

Ordinarily he was not exactly a reckless gambler. He deliberated, followed the run of the luck, and was always at hand to exploit it when it favored him, or to rein himself in when it was another man's turn.

But this evening he soon knew no restraint. No banknote had any value for him. Indeed, it was almost as if he lost with pleasure. Watched with relish as his notes changed sides. Only, something had to keep happening. The cards were dealt far too sluggishly. The naming of the stakes dragged on toward the endless. For him the money crept around the table like sick toads.

On top of it he drank, and all his senses, over which he had lost mastery, turned fiery, like thoroughbred stallions bolting from their coachman on a heath. They ran away with him into a desert. There were no people and no road anymore. Even the air seemed breathed away. In the game he did nothing but fall.

They began to discuss his bad luck. He was getting bad cards, that was certain, but he was also playing badly. He was being unreasonable. From the friendly side of the table they began to curb the play and spoke of last rounds.
Hull did not take in the word at first. It had to be explained to him. Then he balked. He turned abruptly furious, shouted, and pounded his fist on the table.

At that the stranger's great eye drew back a little from him and the others, and seemed to glide inward. Softly, something of its luster went out. The guest laid down the cards and stuffed the money into his pocket; but he did it as incidentally as if it were a handkerchief. One round, however, still remained.
Hull shouted:
Va banque!
The old gentleman dealt the cards. Hull quickly turned his own up for himself. He had twenty-one.
Then something happened in him, something wholly incomprehensible, senseless ... he threw his cards face-down onto the packet of the others that had been pushed aside, and cried:
I've lost again.

Quickly the old gentleman turned up his own cards. His eye flamed once more, going out hastily, quick as lightning. He counted the total, named a figure, and threw his cards into the middle of the table.
To Hull it was as though he were falling from a swaying plank that floated somewhere in a darkness, hung up in invisible things.
Where was I? he asked himself, timid and dumbfounded.

He began to see everything around him anew, as if he were only now stepping into the circle: the three light bulbs, round, dull under the shade, the red cloth in the lamplight, his friends, the strange old gentleman, scattered cards and money.
Where was I? Where was I?
he stammered.
His thoughts awoke, passed from a misty envelopment into a small, sober clarity. It was as though he were pulling draperies off them to undress them.

Then a sudden mistrust of himself seized him and made him sick. For a while he dug his head into his fists, bathed his eyes in the hollows of his hands, which felt as if coated with icy frost, and, straightening up, he said:
What have I done? I had twenty-one! Then someone said with my voice: I have nothing again! ... There ...
He tore the discarded cards off the pile and turned them up.
It was an ace, a ten, and a jack!
Twenty-one!

The old gentleman now drew his great gray eyes entirely into himself. They grew small and looked as if they stood at a great distance. Through the stranger's body there passed, visibly, a violent wrenching, quickly, hastily mastered. Then his chest expanded, and his breath went deep and heavy several times, as if he had to pump air directly into his soul.
Too late!
he then said, soft and stern.
Hull only shook his head.
My remark was not aimed at you,
spans.speaker: Hull

spans.text: he answered, composed again,
but at myself. How much do I owe?
spans.speaker: Hull

spans.text: he asked amiably.
Thirty thousand!
Hull emptied his wallet.

You will have to content yourself until four o'clock tomorrow afternoon with ten thousand marks, and a note of debt, of course. Would you be so kind as to write the address and the sum in my notebook!
When Hull got his book back, it read:
Balling Hotel Excelsior, Room 15.
With a smiling bow he handed over his note of debt in exchange.
Ready to give you your revenge, Herr Hull!
spans.speaker: Balling

spans.text: said Balling, rising.
Gentlemen, may I thank you for the evening's hospitality? Good night!
spans.speaker: Balling

spans.text: He said it in an almost impolite tone, but with a decisiveness that brought the other gentlemen to their feet.
Karstens offered him his car.
No, thank you, my own is waiting for me below.
He went out somewhat stiffly, as if he were wearied, without any further show of courtesy. The club servant led him to the front door.
Hull, you're mad,
spans.speaker: Karstens

spans.text: said Karstens, when the stranger had left the room.
What has actually happened?
spans.speaker: Hull

spans.text: Hull asked calmly in return.
Ask your purse!
spans.speaker: Karstens

spans.text: My wallet is empty. Who won my money?
spans.speaker: Hull

spans.text: Your friend!
spans.speaker: Karstens

spans.text: said Karstens, pointing out the door.
How is he my friend? I'm seeing the man for the first time. How did he get here?
spans.speaker: Hull

spans.text: Hull, decidedly, you need the address of a good doctor. Emil, the telephone directory!
spans.speaker: Karstens

spans.text: Karstens leafed through it:
Here. Dr. Schramm, psycho-pathological treatment, Ludwigstrasse 35 ...
I don't understand your jokes, my dear Karstens!
Well, who brought this magnificent twenty-one player along? You!
That's not true, Karstens!
Ludwigstrasse 35, my dear fellow! Quickly!
Of course you brought him here, Hull,
said another.
I? I? In any case I don't remember it anymore. It may be.
Hull then withdrew, gone slack, astonished, brooding over the riddle this evening had thrown over him so unexpectedly and so brutally.

Toward morning, waking once, there came to him a pale, quickly fading memory: the strange old gentleman seemed to have sat with him at a table in the Café Bastin, and they seemed to have talked together, about the theater, in fact. But what they had said he no longer knew, nor which theater they had discussed. The dark weave of his brain held fast only the flashing sensation of a shrill spotlight that had beamed on him during the conversation. Sleep would not come again, and he burrowed after the gray shreds of these memories; but he could gather up no more.
The experience gained nothing in clarity from what befell Hull on the afternoon of the day following the game.
By four o'clock he had turned the twenty thousand marks liquid and brought them to the Hotel Excelsior.
The desk telephoned up to Room 15.
Herr Balling was in, Hull was told, and requested the gentleman's card. He gave it, and soon went up.
In the middle of Room 15 stood a man Hull had never seen in his life. A small, fat, clean-shaven man with American features. He made a puritanical bow, too.
I must have been shown wrong. Forgive me!
spans.speaker: Hull

spans.text: Hull said to him.
I wanted Room 15.
spans.speaker: Hull

spans.text: You are in it!
the other answered.
Then Herr Balling noted down a wrong number for me.
spans.speaker: Hull

spans.text: My name is Balling!
This time I am not dreaming. I am in full possession of my senses. I am not playing twenty-one, Hull told himself, and then went on aloud to the stranger:
But the riddle will solve itself in a moment. Did you write this?
He held out to Balling his notebook, in which the stranger of the evening before had entered name and address.
No!
the fat man answered.
Then neither have I remained twenty thousand marks in your debt at twenty-one?
My time is short. I am expecting a business associate,
said the fat man, and drew out his watch.
I will leave you to your friend at once, sir, and ask only leave to put one more question. It is not my fault that I am troubling you. I have been misled somehow.
The other nodded.
Hull went on:
Do you then perhaps know a gentleman with large gray eyes, about sixty, white side-whiskers, gray top hat, dressed with discreet elegance, a large nose, and whose name is also Balling?
spans.speaker: Hull

spans.text: I can only go on saying no!
answered the Balling of Room 15.
At that Hull took his leave. Downstairs he asked whether a second Herr Balling was not staying in the hotel.
No!
Whether Room 15 had not perhaps been occupied by a Herr Balling who had since departed ...?
No!
Whether the handwriting here was known?
No!
For the first time in my life I cannot find a man to take a gambling debt off my hands, Hull said to himself as he left the hotel.
Gradually, though, he grew uneasy.

What mysterious connections! Nothing like this had ever happened to him. He had won ... lost ... much and little. He had been in money troubles. He had had bad luck with a girl. He had once fought in earnest with pistols. But all of that you could grasp with your hand, so to speak ...

But this business with Herr Balling and the twenty thousand marks kept fluttering along somewhere behind one. He had forgotten that he himself had brought the stranger into the club. He had played as if his head were in a sack. He had remained twenty thousand marks in debt; the other man gives an address that does exist but is not his own, and he will not even take the money ...?

If Hull had not just then been without a mistress, he could have confided in someone. As it was, he gnawed on it inwardly while he strolled up across the Lenbachplatz and the Promenade, looking everyone in the face in case the distinguished old gentleman should happen to be coming along among them. He went into the Café Bastin and peered under the nose of everyone sitting there. He sat down and waited to see whether, as he put it to himself, the genius loci might lend his memories a helping hand.

But it all ended in a desolate muddle. He found his bearings less and less, and gradually he had a small but tenacious disquiet to contend with. It seemed to him as if a second force ran invisible beside him, a force that had nothing to do with him except that it pressed to perch on him like a monkey and lead him into evil adventures of some kind.
Hull dodged going back to his lonely bachelor flat. Then he met Karstens. Relieved, he hailed him.
But Karstens asked:
Well, has the memory come back to you?
My friend, things are going badly with me!
With the twenty thousand?
Here they are!
He patted his breast pocket.

No, nobody will have them, imagine that. In Room 15 at the Excelsior lives a Herr Balling, but he is not mine. We have never seen each other. He has never played twenty-one, and nobody owes him twenty thousand marks. I cannot get rid of the twenty thousand marks! But in exchange I'm getting the creeps. Something is happening to me. Who is around me? And I don't see him! This will yet end badly for me!
Off to the club! Maybe your Herr Balling will come tonight to collect his money himself!
And the real Herr Balling of Room 15 at the Excelsior?
Yes, man, you do have worries! I grant you that. Come!
Good! Maybe he'll come.
That evening at the club there was no play. The case stirred the imagination to such a degree that nobody needed the pepper of hazard. Hull was heaped with stupid or indifferent advice.
Emil,
one of them asked the servant,
what was his car like, then?

First-class, Herr Baron, a twenty at the very least, closed, elegant, a body like the cradle of a crown prince, if a man may still make that comparison nowadays, so ... rounded, curved, so ... so ... It started off with a leap of five meters and was gone. That car had its twenty-four in it. But I watched his fingers while he was having that filthy luck against Herr von Hull. He played clean.
More than that was not learned about the stranger. Nobody came forward, either at the club or to Hull, to collect the twenty thousand marks or to offer a return match.

The day after, Hull made the acquaintance of a girl who performed grotesque dances at the Bonbonniere. She was of half-Mexican descent, she said. She occupied him amply from the first, distracted him, and with her he quickly freed himself from the pressure of the twenty thousand marks he could not find a man to take.
It was simply fated that you should find a woman to take them,
spans.speaker: Karstens

spans.text: Karstens told him, when Hull informed him of his newly returned lightheartedness.
